title: The right room
hookLine: kindness for the happy, compassion for the hurting, gladness for the successful, equanimity for all

lines: SHE GOT THE JOB. 'I'M SO SORRY.'
THE RIGHT HEART, THE WRONG RESPONSE.
cards: Your friend calls, over the moon: she got the job. You say, oh, I'm so sorry, that must be a lot. There's a pause.
Wrong room. Or your brother calls, crushed, and you say, great, good for you. Wrong room again.
The right heart, the wrong response. Eleven days ago, the four immeasurables became four rooms to live in. Today's question is practical: when someone walks in, which room do you meet them in?

teach.h: EACH QUALITY HAS WHAT CALLS IT UP.
teach.b: Buddhist teachers describe each of the four by what calls it up.

Buddhaghosa, in his Path of Purification, says kindness grows from seeing what is lovable in someone. Compassion, from seeing someone overwhelmed by suffering. Gladness, from seeing someone's success.
Equanimity, from seeing that beings are heirs of their own actions: their lives are finally their own. So there's a natural match.

Kindness is the living room, where anyone can sit, and it fits especially well when someone is simply doing fine: be well, stay well. Compassion is the room for the one who hurts: I see it, and I wish it would end.
Gladness is for the one who's winning: their joy is joy. Equanimity is for everyone.
It's the floor the other three stand on, and where you go when there's nothing left you can do.
The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali have a similar list, naming friendliness toward the happy and compassion toward the suffering; the idea was in the air of ancient India.
Most people have a favorite room. Some live in compassion and treat every bit of good news like a problem. Some live in gladness and can't sit still with someone's grief.
The practice isn't picking your best room. It's noticing who just walked in, and opening the right door.

how: Buddhist teachers often pair each brahmavihara with the situation that calls for it, compassion for suffering and gladness for success, and practitioners use the four as a way to meet people as they actually are that day.

o: gladness at someone else's good fortune
pride in your own hard-won success
a cheerful mood that comes from nowhere

games.q: match each room to who walks in.

s: the practice is to find your one best room and stay there
it's to notice who walked in and open the door that fits.
Buddhaghosa says equanimity grows from seeing beings as heirs of their own actions
their lives are finally their own.
a similar list appears in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering: the idea was shared in ancient India.

games.q: your friend calls, thrilled: she got the job you both applied for. which room do you open?
o: compassion: 'that must be so much pressure.'
games.why: success calls up gladness. equanimity helps you with your own sting, but the door she needs is gladness.

practice: Think of one person you'll probably talk to today and ask: how are they, really? Doing fine, hurting, celebrating something, or facing something no one can fix?
Pick the room that fits, kindness, compassion, gladness or equanimity, and rest there with them in mind for a few breaths, as if the door is open and they're walking in.

wordCard.voice: Muditā. Gladness at another's good fortune: kindness is for anyone, compassion for the hurting, muditā for the glad, equanimity underneath it all.

orig.note: Pali muditā: gladness at another's good fortune, the room for success.

carryVoice: Your line: notice who just walked in. Good news and hard news knock on different doors. Day two hundred forty-three, done.
